questions.stem: A healthy patient completed a phone preanesthesia interview 12 days ago. The chart is complete and nothing has changed. Which requirement still cannot be omitted on the morning of surgery?
options: A repeat interview only if laboratory values changed
No further interview because the phone assessment remains valid
An in-person clinic interview because the prior assessment was remote
questions.explanation: The preoperative assessment can occur 1–30 days ahead, including by phone, but a day-of-surgery interview is still required.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A stable elective patient has no major comorbidity and will be assessed by phone rather than in clinic. Which scheduling interval is consistent with the preoperative assessment process?
questions.explanation: The preoperative assessment window is 1–30 days before surgery, followed by a day-of-surgery interview.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An elective colectomy patient has EF 25%, stage 4 CKD, and insulin-dependent diabetes but is not acutely decompensated. What timing best preserves an opportunity for optimization rather than merely identifying risk on the day of surgery?
options: At least a week before surgery
Any time within 30 days if symptoms develop
questions.explanation: Medically complex patients should visit the preop testing center at least a week before surgery so testing and optimization can happen and preventable cancellations are avoided.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A hospital is deciding whether an in-person preoperative testing clinic adds value beyond a day-of-surgery interview. Which benefits justify the clinic? (Select 4)
options: Consolidated testing such as labs, imaging, and other studies
Time to optimize medical conditions before surgery
Replacement of the surgeon's history and physical
questions.explanation: Early visits educate, consolidate testing, allow optimization, and reduce preventable cancellations. They do not replace the day-of interview or the surgeon's H&P.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 66-year-old takes metoprolol, lisinopril, furosemide, and glipizide. To avoid rebound sympathetic effects without increasing common peri-induction medication risks, which drug should be taken with a sip of water?
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers are continued to avoid rebound tachycardia and ischemia. ACE inhibitors, diuretics, and oral hypoglycemics are held.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes losartan, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. Which morning-of-surgery plan best avoids medication-related hypotension or volume depletion while maintaining usual antihypertensive therapy?
options: Take amlodipine; hold losartan and hydrochlorothiazide
Take losartan; hold amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide
Take hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine; hold losartan
questions.explanation: Most antihypertensives are taken, but ARBs, ACE inhibitors, and diuretics are held. Losartan and HCTZ are held; amlodipine is taken.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 68-year-old takes lisinopril 40 mg every morning, including today, and is induced with propofol 150 mg. BP falls to 68/35 and responds only briefly to phenylephrine. What mechanism BEST explains this?
options: Lisinopril causes direct myocardial depression with propofol
Lisinopril causes hyperkalemia that depresses contractility
questions.explanation: With the renin-angiotensin system blocked, the patient cannot compensate for anesthetic vasodilation, so hypotension is refractory to standard pressors. This is why ACE inhibitors and ARBs are commonly held.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: One patient has a drug-eluting coronary stent and takes aspirin plus clopidogrel; another takes rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation. Which management principle applies to both before surgery?
options: Individualize interruption or continuation by balancing bleeding and thrombosis
Continue both drug classes through surgery as a fixed rule
Hold both drug classes only on the morning of surgery as a fixed rule
Replace either regimen with low-dose aspirin the day before surgery
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets are managed case by case, balancing surgical and neuraxial bleeding risk against thrombotic risk such as stent thrombosis.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease and a seizure disorder is NPO for surgery and asks whether carbidopa-levodopa and levetiracetam should be skipped. Which instruction best prevents avoidable perioperative deterioration?
options: Take both on the morning of surgery
Hold both to minimize anesthetic interactions
questions.explanation: Antiseizure and Parkinson's medications are on the "take" list. Stopping them risks seizures or rigidity and aspiration.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 70-year-old takes furosemide, glyburide, a multivitamin, fish oil, an albuterol inhaler, and metoprolol. Which four are ordinarily held on the morning of surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Hold diuretics, oral hypoglycemics, and vitamins or herbals. Inhalers and beta-blockers are taken.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes oxycodone 10 mg every 8 hours chronically and is scheduled for a painful laminectomy. Which morning-of-surgery instruction best limits withdrawal and worsening postoperative analgesic requirements?
options: Hold the dose to reduce intraoperative respiratory depression
Take half of the usual dose
Hold the dose and substitute only a postoperative PCA
questions.explanation: Home opioids are continued. Stopping them risks withdrawal and makes postoperative pain harder to control.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Which preoperative action best reflects the purpose of evaluation rather than simply completing documentation?
options: Identify modifiable risk, prepare the patient, and build an anesthetic plan
Diagnose every untreated disease, order routine labs, and schedule surgery
Obtain consent, administer premedication, and start an IV
Assign ASA class, calculate one risk score, and determine staffing
questions.explanation: Preoperative evaluation aims to reduce risk and morbidity, prepare the patient medically and psychologically, and develop a comprehensive plan.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: You begin chart review for the first case of the day. Which verification comes before interpreting comorbidities, laboratory values, or prior anesthetic records?
options: Patient identity and the planned procedure
Risk stratification and the provisional anesthetic plan
The most recent laboratory values and imaging
questions.explanation: Chart review begins by confirming patient ID and procedure, then moves to history, prior anesthetic records, labs, risk, consent, allergies, and medications.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A prior anesthetic record documents a grade 4 laryngoscopic view with successful bougie-assisted video laryngoscopy. What should this finding change before induction?
options: Prepare a difficult-airway strategy and equipment in advance
Document it but begin with the usual airway plan
Use rapid-sequence induction with a Mac 4 blade as the default first attempt
Choose regional anesthesia solely to avoid airway management
questions.explanation: Identifying previous intubation notes and difficult airways is a chart review essential. It should drive equipment and plan, such as VL and the difficult airway cart.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 72-year-old reports severe postoperative nausea and vomiting and two days of confusion after a prior anesthetic. Which additional anesthesia-history elements belong in the same focused review? (Select 4)
options: Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: The anesthesia history covers difficult airway, PONV, emergence delirium or slow emergence, and personal or family history of MH.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient's father developed marked hyperthermia and muscle rigidity during anesthesia and nearly died. Which interpretation has the greatest anesthetic consequence?
options: This is anesthesia history suggesting possible familial malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
This is social history suggesting postoperative alcohol withdrawal risk
This is cardiac history predicting perioperative ischemia
This is family history primarily suggesting pseudocholinesterase deficiency
questions.explanation: Family history of MH is flagged in the anesthesia history section. It may require a trigger-free technique.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: The chart lists no prior anesthetic complications, but the patient recalls awakening after surgery, becoming severely dyspneic, and requiring reintubation. What is the most important lesson for the current evaluation?
options: Important anesthetic complications may be absent from the existing chart
The prior chart should no longer be used for planning
Patient recollection should replace review of previous records
The interview removes the need for formal consent
questions.explanation: The interview captures history and complications that may not be documented, and it verifies medications and allergies.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: One patient lists codeine as an allergy because of nausea and pruritus; another reports penicillin-associated hives and lip swelling. What distinction should be explicitly documented because it changes how each entry is interpreted?
questions.explanation: Allergy verification separates immune-mediated reactions (hives, angioedema) from non-immune side effects (nausea, itching from histamine release).
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: You have limited time for a focused day-of-surgery examination before an uncomplicated hernia repair. Which examination set is most aligned with anesthesia-specific risk detection?
options: Airway, neurologic, cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal
Airway, cardiovascular, renal, skin, and musculoskeletal
Neurologic, cardiovascular, endocrine, renal, and gastrointestinal
Airway, pulmonary, hematologic, renal, and skin
questions.explanation: The modified physical assessment includes airway, neuro, cardiovascular, pulmonary, and GI on the day of surgery.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient had a complete preoperative clinic examination two weeks ago but now reports new bilateral ankle swelling. What is required before induction?
options: A focused day-of-surgery physical addressing the interval change
No further examination because a full physical was already completed
A repeat complete physical only if laboratory values also changed
questions.explanation: The modified physical (airway, neuro, CV, pulmonary, GI) is done on the day of surgery, which is how new findings like edema are caught.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A healthy ambulatory patient has a responsible adult available to drive home after anesthesia, but no one can stay with the patient afterward. Which discharge-planning issue should be identified before proceeding?
options: No responsible adult is available for the first 24 hours after anesthesia
Transportation home is adequate, so no additional support is needed
A family member must be present during induction
The surgical consent requires a relative's signature
questions.explanation: The slide says ask who is present and who will be there to care for them at least 24 hours after anesthesia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: The chart already documents OSA on CPAP, diabetes, and a previous difficult intubation. With limited preoperative interview time, which approach best reduces the chance of missing a new risk?
options: Verify the known high-risk findings, then deliberately probe for gaps or interval changes
Repeat the entire history without using the chart
Ask only about diagnoses already listed in the chart
Review abnormal chart items and omit questions about unchanged systems
questions.explanation: Covering known issues first, then probing for missing information, balances efficiency with completeness.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An SRNA repeatedly omits important preoperative questions when cases become busy. Which change most directly reduces omission errors without replacing clinical judgment?
options: Use a consistent structured interview template
Use a scripted consent video before each case
Rely on the preoperative order set to capture the history
Substitute a patient questionnaire for the interview
questions.explanation: The preop interview takes practice, and a personal template early in training keeps it complete and consistent.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: At the start of the preoperative interview, which form of address best follows the lecture's strategy for establishing professional rapport?
options: Address the patient by surname unless invited to do otherwise
Use the patient's first name immediately to appear informal
Use a nickname if one is visible in the chart
Avoid using the patient's name until consent is signed
questions.explanation: The slide advises using the surname to show respect along with a professional attitude and introduction.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 74-year-old takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty with a planned spinal. Which principle should drive the perioperative anticoagulation plan?
options: Balance thromboembolic risk against surgical and neuraxial bleeding risk
Continue apixaban through surgery because atrial fibrillation is chronic
Hold only the morning dose and proceed with spinal anesthesia
Replace apixaban with aspirin the day before surgery
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants are managed case by case. Timing must account for surgical bleeding, neuraxial hematoma risk, and thrombotic risk.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Three weeks before elective hip replacement, a patient reports exertional chest pain and subsequent testing demonstrates inducible ischemia. Which function of the preoperative process is most clearly demonstrated?
options: Identifying a problem early enough for additional evaluation or optimization
Improving operating-room turnover by completing testing early
Replacing the surgeon's history and physical examination
Determining whether the patient can be discharged the same day
questions.explanation: Perioperative evaluation identifies patients who need further testing or optimization before surgery, reducing risk.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A fasting patient accidentally takes the usual morning glipizide dose before surgery. Which immediate preoperative risk should receive priority surveillance?
questions.explanation: Oral hypoglycemics are held because a fasting patient can become hypoglycemic. Check glucose and monitor.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A facility allows physicians, CRNAs, NPs, and PAs to perform the formal preanesthesia assessment. A preoperative holding RN offers to complete it independently. Which statement is correct?
options: The RN may collect data but is not one of the listed clinicians who may perform the formal assessment
The RN may perform it if the patient is ASA I or II
The RN may perform it when a CRNA cosigns later
The RN may perform it for regional anesthesia but not general anesthesia
questions.explanation: The preanesthesia assessment may be done by an MD, CRNA, NP, or PA, but not by an RN.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A chart carries a difficult-airway alert, but the patient cannot recall details. Which two chart elements are most important to review before finalizing the airway plan? (Select 2)
options: Current consent, allergies, and medication list
questions.explanation: Chart review covers ID, procedure, prior records including intubation notes, labs, risk stratification, consent, allergies, and medications.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient reports that after a prior anesthetic he became apneic in PACU and required prolonged respiratory support. Which preoperative interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Treat it as an anesthesia-history signal for conditions such as OSA or heightened respiratory-depressant sensitivity
Classify it only as a medication-history issue from benzodiazepine exposure
Classify it as social history suggesting substance misuse
Classify it as surgical history because it occurred after the operation
questions.explanation: Postop respiratory events are anesthesia history. They raise concern for OSA or opioid sensitivity and change monitoring and analgesia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An 81-year-old was confused and not at baseline for three days after a previous anesthetic. Where should this information be captured because it may alter the current anesthetic and recovery plan?
options: Prior anesthesia history, including postoperative delirium or delayed recovery
Medication history as an isolated opioid adverse effect
questions.explanation: Emergence delirium or slow emergence belongs in the anesthesia history, especially in elderly patients who are at higher risk.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has never received anesthesia and has no documented drug allergies. Which conclusion is safest during preoperative planning?
options: Absence of prior exposure means reactions to common anesthetic drugs or antibiotics are still unknown
The patient is at increased PONV risk but not at risk for drug reactions
The patient will require a higher volatile anesthetic concentration
The patient should automatically be classified ASA II
questions.explanation: The allergy slide says use caution with a patient who has never had anesthesia because reactions to common triggers are unknown.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and presents with a hip fracture and INR 3.1. Which approach best reflects the competing perioperative risks?
options: Coordinate an individualized plan for reversal, timing, and thromboembolic protection
Continue warfarin unchanged and treat bleeding only if it occurs
Stop warfarin and proceed immediately without further planning
Replace warfarin with aspirin and proceed
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants are case by case. With a mechanical valve, reversal, bridging, and timing must be planned with the surgical and cardiology teams.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient was considered low risk three weeks ago, but this morning potassium is 6.1 mEq/L with new peaked T waves. What must the day-of-surgery review do first with the prior assessment?
options: Reassess whether the previous risk stratification and anesthetic plan remain valid
Confirm only that surgical consent is signed
Confirm NPO status and keep the prior plan unchanged
Accept the original plan because it was completed within 30 days
questions.explanation: Day-of-surgery chart review verifies that the risk stratification and plan are still valid; new hyperkalemia changes both.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: Which history should trigger the largest change in anesthetic preparation before an otherwise routine elective case?
options: A first-degree relative developed severe hyperthermia and rigidity during anesthesia
The patient had mild nausea after a previous dental anesthetic
The patient has seasonal allergic rhinitis
The patient had an uncomplicated appendectomy years ago
questions.explanation: A family history suggestive of MH requires a trigger-free anesthetic. The others may adjust the plan but do not change the technique.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation misses the usual morning metoprolol dose and arrives with HR 118/min. Which consequence best explains why chronic beta-blocker therapy is ordinarily continued?
options: Loss of rate control with rebound sympathetic activity and greater myocardial oxygen demand
Prolonged neuromuscular blockade from beta-receptor upregulation
Refractory vasodilatory hypotension from beta-blocker withdrawal
Reduced MAC requirement from acute beta-blocker discontinuation
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers are taken to avoid withdrawal tachycardia and ischemia.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient consents to general anesthesia with an LMA after hearing only the planned technique; possible intubation and neuraxial alternatives were not discussed. Which element of informed consent is deficient?
options: Meaningful discussion of material risks and reasonable alternatives
The consent was signed after, rather than before, the discussion
Regional anesthesia is not an alternative that needs discussion
Airway risks are covered automatically by the surgical consent
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires discussing risks, benefits, and options, including alternatives such as neuraxial or regional techniques.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty. Which anesthetic option deserves explicit discussion because it may reduce the need for airway instrumentation and systemic respiratory depressants?
options: General anesthesia because it is mandatory for knee surgery
Routine postoperative ICU admission regardless of technique
questions.explanation: The plan discussion should include neuraxial or regional options, which can avoid airway instrumentation in a patient with severe COPD.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: After evaluating a patient with OSA and coronary disease for colectomy, which three decisions belong directly in the anesthesia plan generated from the assessment? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The preoperative assessment leads to a plan covering premedication, monitoring, positioning, and equipment setup.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient takes St. John's wort, ginkgo, and vitamin E before a spine procedure. Which instruction best addresses medication-interaction and bleeding concerns?
options: Hold the vitamins and herbal products before surgery
Continue all three to prevent withdrawal
Take half-doses on the morning of surgery
Continue ginkgo but hold St. John's wort and vitamin E
questions.explanation: Vitamins and herbals are held. Ginkgo and vitamin E can increase bleeding, and St. John's wort induces drug metabolism.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient discloses during the interview that she has hepatitis C and a history of IV drug use. Which purpose of the preop evaluation does this information directly serve?
options: Assessing risk to patient and provider
questions.explanation: The preop evaluation assesses risk to the patient and the provider, such as bloodborne pathogen exposure.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient seems guarded and gives short answers in preop. Why does a professional introduction at the start of the interview matter?
options: It builds trust for an honest history and valid consent
It shortens the total interview time
It replaces the need for a chart review
It shortens the time needed for the interview
questions.explanation: A respectful introduction builds trust, which improves the accuracy of the history and the quality of informed consent.
questions.topic: Preop process, chart review, and home medications

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for an ankle fracture repair under a popliteal block with minimal sedation. Why is a full airway exam still required?
options: Any plan may need emergent airway control
The block may need supplemental sedation
It determines the local anesthetic dose
Regional failure rates are higher in fracture patients
questions.explanation: Any anesthetic can progress to needing airway rescue, so the airway is evaluated for every patient.

questions.stem: A patient has Mallampati II, three-fingerbreadth mouth opening, a full beard, a short thick neck, and limited extension. Each finding alone is minor. How should you interpret the exam?
options: The findings combine to predict a difficult airway
The airway is normal, since Mallampati is II
The beard is the finding that matters
The neck extension is the finding that matters
questions.explanation: Several minor findings can combine to create difficulty with mask ventilation and laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient has a full beard, BMI 38, and a Mallampati III. Which lecture planning step BEST fits?
options: Prepare video laryngoscopy, positioning aids, and the airway cart
Proceed with standard setup since no single finding is severe
Plan awake fiberoptic intubation for every patient like this
Cancel until the beard is shaved
questions.explanation: Anticipating a difficult airway means planning VL, positioning aids, and the difficult airway cart.

questions.stem: You are examining the airway of a 60-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis. Which structures should you inspect?
options: Teeth, mouth, mandibular space, and neck
Teeth, tongue, chest wall, and neck
questions.explanation: The airway exam inspects the teeth, mouth, mandibular space, and neck.

questions.stem: A patient has acromegaly, another has a large goiter, and a third has Pierre Robin sequence. How are these airway concerns categorized?
options: Cardiac, pulmonary, and renal disease processes
questions.explanation: Airway problems fall into structural features, metabolic diseases, and congenital or acquired anomalies.

questions.stem: A patient with Parkinson's disease is scheduled for surgery. Which neuro history item should you document?
questions.explanation: The neuro slide lists CVA, Parkinson's, or essential tremor history. Baseline tremor and medications matter for planning.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with epilepsy is scheduled for a shoulder repair. Which seizure history is MOST useful for planning?
options: Type, frequency, triggers, medications, and last episode
Last episode alone, since it predicts intraop risk
Seizure type alone, since medications are charted
Medication list alone, since triggers do not apply
questions.explanation: A useful seizure history includes type, frequency, triggers, medications, and the last episode.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old had a stroke two years ago and is scheduled for a carotid endarterectomy. What must you document before surgery?
options: Baseline motor weakness or other deficits
Lower extremity deep tendon reflexes alone
questions.explanation: After a TIA or stroke, document baseline motor weakness or deficits so new postoperative deficits can be recognized.

questions.stem: A patient reports neuralgia in the extremities. What does this change?
questions.explanation: Extremity neuralgia may require careful positioning to avoid worsening.

questions.stem: Which are delirium and postoperative cognitive risk factors on the neuro slide? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Risk factors include advanced age, baseline cognitive impairment, prior delirium, sensory impairment, polypharmacy, and alcohol or sedative use.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with hearing loss, mild dementia, and 11 home medications is booked for a hip repair. Which risk is MOST emphasized in the neuro section?
questions.explanation: Age, cognitive impairment, sensory loss, and polypharmacy are listed delirium risk factors.

questions.stem: Which patients need a detailed neuro exam before surgery? (Select 2)
options: A patient with diabetic neuropathy before a popliteal block
A patient scheduled for carotid endarterectomy
A healthy patient for cataract surgery
A healthy patient for dental extraction
A patient for laparoscopic cholecystectomy with no neuro history
A healthy adult for hernia repair
questions.explanation: Detailed neuro exams are needed with regional anesthesia when deficits exist, carotid or vascular surgery, intracranial or spine surgery, recent stroke, high delirium risk, and altered mental status.

questions.stem: Why is a detailed neuro exam important before regional anesthesia in a patient with baseline deficits?
options: It documents a baseline to compare postop findings
It proves regional anesthesia is contraindicated
questions.explanation: Documenting pre-existing deficits separates old findings from new injury after regional anesthesia.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for carotid endarterectomy has a recent TIA. Which is the MOST appropriate preop step?
options: Perform and document a detailed neuro exam
Rely on the neurologist's note from the TIA admission
Document the airway exam before carotid surgery
questions.explanation: Carotid surgery and recent TIA are both listed situations needing a detailed neuro exam.

questions.stem: The notes say "anesthesia is the airway expert." What does this imply for MAC or regional cases?
options: Airway evaluation is needed if conversion is planned
Airway evaluation is done by the surgeon
Airway evaluation is done when GA is planned
questions.explanation: Airway assessment is essential regardless of anesthesia plan.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old drinks a pint of vodka daily and takes alprazolam 2 mg at night. He needs a far larger midazolam dose than expected, then becomes apneic after one more small dose. Which history should have shaped your dosing?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol and sedative use alter tolerance and response, requiring careful titration.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with new confusion and a subdural hematoma needs urgent surgery. What exam is required before induction?
options: A six-week delay for neuro recovery
questions.explanation: Altered mental status requires a detailed neuro exam to establish a baseline before surgery.

questions.stem: A patient with a Mallampati IV airway and limited neck extension is scheduled for a thyroidectomy. Which preparation BEST fits the anticipated difficult airway?
options: A videolaryngoscope and the difficult airway cart
A nasogastric tube, suction, and a standard blade
questions.explanation: Anticipating a difficult airway means preparing a VL, positioning aids, and the difficult airway cart.

questions.stem: Four patients are on today's schedule. Which one MOST needs a detailed neuro exam before surgery?
options: An 84-year-old with dementia at high delirium risk
A healthy 45-year-old for inguinal hernia repair
questions.explanation: Elderly patients at high risk of delirium need a detailed neuro baseline.

questions.stem: A patient has an essential tremor. Why does this matter?
options: It sets a baseline and may affect regional or positioning plans
It predicts difficult laryngoscopy from tremor
It raises the risk of malignant hyperthermia with volatile triggers
It contraindicates regional anesthesia in that limb
questions.explanation: Neuro disorders like essential tremor are part of the baseline neuro history.

questions.stem: The preop airway exam is reassuring in one patient and concerning in another. Which outcome does the exam help predict?
questions.explanation: The airway exam predicts difficult mask ventilation and intubation, which guides equipment and backup plans.

questions.stem: A patient has a history of migraines triggered by bright light and stress. Which item does the neuro slide ask you to document?
options: Triggers, frequency, medications, and last episode
Whether they are migraines with or without aura
questions.explanation: The neuro slide asks about type, frequency, triggers, medications, and last episode.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old is scheduled for a cervical laminectomy for myelopathy. Which preop exam is indicated beyond the standard assessment?
options: A cardiac exam in place of the neuro exam
A pulmonary exam in place of the neuro exam
An airway exam in place of the neuro exam
questions.explanation: Intracranial or spine surgery calls for a detailed neuro exam to document baseline deficits.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has a full beard, a short thick neck, and three fingerbreadths of mouth opening, with Mallampati II. How should you interpret this exam?
options: Several minor findings can add up to a difficult airway
The airway is normal since Mallampati is II
The beard matters most and the neck is less relevant
Mouth opening of three fingerbreadths rules out difficulty
questions.explanation: Multiple minor abnormalities, such as a beard and short neck, can combine to make mask ventilation or intubation difficult.

questions.stem: A patient has prior neck radiation. Which lecture category does this fit?
questions.explanation: Acquired anomalies include changes from radiation or surgery that can make the airway difficult.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old takes 14 medications, including diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, and lorazepam, and is at high delirium risk. Which risk factor is MOST modifiable before surgery?
questions.explanation: Polypharmacy can be reduced before surgery by stopping or substituting deliriogenic drugs; age and baseline cognition cannot be changed.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old's hands shake when holding a cup, worse with action, and she takes propranolol. Which neurologic history item is this?
questions.explanation: Neurologic history includes CVA, Parkinson's disease, and essential tremor. Note the propranolol as a home beta-blocker.

questions.stem: A patient with an old stroke and left arm weakness is having a right shoulder block. What is the BEST preop action?
options: Document baseline weakness before the block
Avoid the block because of prior stroke
Document strength after the block for comparison
Use GA to avoid any neuro changes
questions.explanation: Regional anesthesia with pre-existing deficits is a listed situation; baseline documentation protects the patient and provider.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old with cataracts and hearing aids is scheduled for hip surgery. Why do these sensory impairments matter?
options: They impair orientation and raise delirium risk
They predict a difficult airway and mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Hearing and vision impairment make orientation harder after surgery and are delirium risk factors. Keep glasses and hearing aids available in PACU.

questions.stem: A patient for a carpal tunnel release under WALANT asks why you are looking in her mouth. What is the BEST explanation?
options: Any plan may need airway rescue
The airway exam determines the local dose
The surgeon requires it for WALANT
questions.explanation: The airway is evaluated for every patient because any plan can require emergent airway control.

questions.stem: A 70 kg patient's oxygen consumption at rest is about 245 mL/min. Climbing two flights of stairs raises it to about 1,000 mL/min. Roughly how many METs is that activity?
questions.explanation: One MET is about 3.5 mL/kg/min, or about 245 mL/min for 70 kg. 1,000 mL/min ÷ 245 mL/min is about 4 METs.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old scheduled for a hip replacement walks two miles daily and does yard work without symptoms. What does his functional capacity suggest?
options: Good capacity above 4 METs, with adequate reserve
Poor capacity below 4 METs, needing stress testing
Good capacity once he exceeds 10 METs
questions.explanation: More than 4 METs indicates good functional capacity and adequate cardiopulmonary reserve.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old says he climbs two flights of stairs daily without chest pain or dyspnea and has no unstable cardiac disease. What is the BEST interpretation for elective surgery?
options: ≥4 METs; further cardiac testing usually not needed
≥4 METs; stress testing still required due to age
Capacity unclear; delay until an echo is done
questions.explanation: Climbing two flights without symptoms shows ≥4 METs. Without unstable disease, additional testing is usually not required.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old says she can do several activities without symptoms. Which one BEST shows she can achieve at least 4 METs?
options: Scrubbing floors or moving heavy furniture
questions.explanation: Heavy housework, two flights of stairs or a hill, and moderate to strenuous activity show at least 4 METs.

questions.stem: A patient can dress and walk around her house but stops halfway up one flight of stairs because of dyspnea. What does this indicate?
options: <4 METs; consider further cardiac risk assessment
≥4 METs, since she can do housework
Normal capacity for her age; no action needed
Pulmonary limitation, so cardiac risk is lower
questions.explanation: Failing stairs because of dyspnea means reduced capacity (<4 METs), which prompts further assessment per guidelines.

questions.stem: A colleague charts "5 METs" for a patient based only on his description of yard work. How should this value be understood?
options: A subjective estimate of cardiopulmonary capacity
An objective value measured by CPET
An objective value derived from echo EF
A value calculated from BMI and resting HR
questions.explanation: METs from history are a subjective estimate. Objective measures come from exercise testing or CPET.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old's functional capacity is unclear from history. Which tests give an objective measure?
questions.explanation: Exercise testing or CPET objectively measures functional capacity.

questions.stem: Two patients have the same surgery. One can walk only to the mailbox before stopping; the other jogs daily. What does the first patient's capacity predict?
questions.explanation: Poor cardiopulmonary capacity is associated with increased perioperative risk.

questions.stem: Which activities show ≥4 METs? (Select 2)
options: Walking one block on level ground
questions.explanation: Singles tennis and walking up a hill reach at least 4 METs. Walking one block on level ground, desk work, and washing dishes are below 4 METs.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old seems puzzled when asked about climbing stairs. Which questions would BEST estimate her METs?
options: Shopping, walking store to store, pushing a mower
Hours of sleep, naps, and night awakenings
Driving distance and time behind the wheel
Meals per day and recent weight change
questions.explanation: Age-appropriate questions such as shopping, walking the mall, and pushing a mower estimate METs more reliably in older patients.

questions.stem: A patient has never had a stress test, but he climbs two flights of stairs daily without symptoms. Why is this information useful?
options: It replaces the need for an airway exam
questions.explanation: Functional capacity is a surrogate marker of cardiopulmonary reserve before surgery.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old with diabetes and hypertension cannot walk far because of severe knee arthritis and is scheduled for an elevated-risk procedure. What is the BEST next step?
options: Treat capacity as unclear and pursue further risk assessment
Assume more than 4 METs since the limit is orthopedic
Assume less than 4 METs and order a stress test for everyone
Proceed, since orthopedic limitation does not reflect cardiac risk
questions.explanation: Capacity below 4 METs or unclear capacity prompts further cardiac risk assessment per guidelines.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old walks briskly up two flights of stairs daily but reports new chest pain at rest last week. Can additional cardiac testing be skipped?
options: No; he has an unstable cardiac condition
Yes, since stair climbing shows good capacity
Yes, since his METs exceed 4 on stair climbing
Yes, if his ASA class is II
questions.explanation: Good capacity usually means no further testing, provided there is no unstable cardiac disease. New rest angina is unstable.

questions.stem: A patient runs 3 miles weekly but reported new chest pain at rest last week. What is the BEST next step?
options: Evaluate the active cardiac symptoms before surgery
Proceed since functional capacity is excellent
Proceed after a single normal ECG
Treat as low risk because of exercise tolerance
questions.explanation: Good capacity does not cancel active cardiac conditions like new rest angina. Those require evaluation.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old has an RCRI of 1, 5 METs, and is ASA III. How should these three measures be used together?
options: Combined to estimate overall risk and guide testing
RCRI alone decides whether surgery proceeds
METs alone decide whether surgery proceeds
ASA class alone decides whether surgery proceeds
questions.explanation: METs, RCRI, and ASA status are used together, since none fully captures risk alone.

questions.stem: The notes say "<4 METs = further cardiac assessment." What does this mean practically?
options: Proceed, since risk is driven by the procedure
questions.explanation: Reduced capacity prompts further cardiac risk assessment, which may include testing or consultation.

questions.stem: A patient scrubs floors and swims weekly without symptoms. Which conclusion is BEST?
options: Capacity is uncertain without a stress test
questions.explanation: Heavy household work and swimming are ≥4 MET activities.

questions.stem: A patient says he "walks a lot," but his wife says he gets short of breath after half a block. Which limitation of METs does this show?
options: METs are subjective and depend on patient report
METs are measured objectively by echo
METs predict pulmonary complications rather than cardiac
questions.explanation: METs from history are subjective and can be over- or underestimated; objective testing such as CPET is more reliable.

questions.stem: Which patient BEST fits "poor functional capacity"?
options: Unable to climb one flight of stairs
One who climbs one flight slowly without symptoms
One who scrubs floors without symptoms
One who walks up a hill daily without stopping
questions.explanation: Inability to climb stairs due to fatigue and dyspnea indicates less than 4 METs, or poor capacity.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old reports carrying groceries up two flights of stairs without symptoms and has no active cardiac conditions. What does this suggest?
options: More than 4 METs, suggesting adequate reserve
Less than 4 METs, requiring stress testing
questions.explanation: More than 4 METs suggests sufficient cardiopulmonary reserve; testing is usually not needed without active disease.

questions.stem: A patient had a drug-eluting stent placed 4 months ago and is scheduled for an elective cholecystectomy. What is the BEST plan?
options: Proceed if 3–6 months have passed, continuing aspirin
Proceed and stop aspirin 7 days before
Delay until 12 months and stop all antiplatelets
Proceed after stopping DAPT for 60 days
questions.explanation: Elective surgery after a DES is acceptable at 3–6 months with aspirin continued to reduce stent thrombosis.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a bare metal stent placed 5 weeks ago and needs an elective hernia repair. Is the timing acceptable?
options: Yes, since more than 30 days have passed
Yes, since 7 days is enough for any stent type
questions.explanation: Elective surgery can proceed more than 30 days after a bare metal stent.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had an MI 5 weeks ago treated medically without PCI or surgery and is scheduled for an elective knee replacement. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Delay at least 60 days from the MI
Proceed if METs exceed 4 by history
questions.explanation: After an MI managed without intervention, wait at least 60 days before elective surgery.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had CABG 4 months ago and wants an elective shoulder replacement. What is the BEST advice?
options: Wait until more than 6 months after CABG
questions.explanation: Elective surgery should wait more than 6 months after CABG.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a DES placed 7 weeks ago and is on aspirin and clopidogrel. The surgeon wants to stop both for an elective hernia repair next week. What is the BEST response?
options: Advise delay; DES timing and DAPT make this unsafe
Proceed after stopping both drugs for 5 days
Proceed and restart DAPT in PACU
Proceed if an ECG is normal today
questions.explanation: DES patients are on DAPT and elective surgery is delayed 3–6 months with aspirin continued. Stopping DAPT early risks stent thrombosis.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: The notes describe the MI that "requires no intervention" as which type?
questions.explanation: Type II MI results from supply-demand imbalance, such as anemia or sepsis hypotension, and is not fixed by PCI.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A 60-year-old is scheduled for a femoral bypass. Which findings in his history are risk factors for ischemic heart disease? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: IHD risk factors include age, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, and PVD. Hypothyroidism is not on this list.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Patient A has had exertional chest pain at the same level for 3 years. Patient B has had new chest pain at rest twice this week. Both are scheduled for elective knee replacements. How should they be managed?
options: A may proceed; B needs cardiac evaluation first
B may proceed; A needs cardiac evaluation first
questions.explanation: Stable angina is not an active condition, but new rest angina is unstable and needs evaluation before elective surgery.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A 62-year-old's stress test is equivocal and the cardiologist wants a definitive answer about coronary disease before a major vascular case. Which test provides it?
questions.explanation: Cardiac catheterization provides definitive information about coronary anatomy.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with severe knee arthritis cannot walk a block and needs stress testing before an aortic repair. Which test is appropriate?
options: Pharmacologic stress with dobutamine or adenosine
Treadmill stress at a lower workload
Tilt-table testing with continuous ECG recording
questions.explanation: Patients who cannot exercise can have pharmacologic stress testing with dipyridamole, adenosine, or dobutamine.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with CAD says, "My cardiologist saw me last month." What is the MOST useful next step in your assessment?
options: Find the recent cardiology note or clearance
Ask whether he takes a statin
Ask how much coffee he drinks
Order a chest X-ray if none in the past year
questions.explanation: A recent cardiology note or clearance gives current function, testing, and recommendations that guide your plan.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Two patients are scheduled for a colectomy: one with an EF of 55% and one with an EF of 30%. How does the lower EF change your assessment?
options: It matters mainly if the procedure is cardiac surgery
It lowers anesthetic requirements without changing risk
questions.explanation: An EF below 40% signals higher perioperative risk and affects drug choice, monitoring, and fluid management.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient's preop BP is 148/94 on two readings. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Stage 2 is ≥140/≥90. Stage 1 is 130–139/80–89, and elevated is 120–129/<80.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient's BP is 162/98 on the morning of elective surgery with no symptoms or end-organ damage. Which lecture statement BEST guides the decision?
options: BP <180/<110 is not an independent risk predictor
Stage 2 hypertension requires a cardiology consult
BP over 160 systolic requires a beta-blocker bolus
questions.explanation: The slide states <180/<110 is not an independent predictor of CV complications. Assess end-organ damage and symptoms.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A 61-year-old's BP is 168/98 in preop. Which questions BEST assess his hypertension? (Select 3)
options: Has he had syncope or dizziness?
Which medications, doses, and last dose time?
What was his BP at the last dental visit?
Does he prefer a left or right arm cuff?
Is his BP higher at night than in the morning?
questions.explanation: Hypertension assessment focuses on end-organ dysfunction, symptoms, and the medication list with timing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient takes lisinopril, amlodipine, metoprolol, and chlorthalidone, all this morning. Why does the number of antihypertensives and their timing matter?
questions.explanation: Multiple agents taken the same morning, especially ACE inhibitors and diuretics, predict hypotension after induction.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient has a DES from 8 months ago and is on aspirin only. What is the BEST plan for elective surgery?
questions.explanation: After 3–6 months with a DES, elective surgery can proceed with aspirin continued.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with a remote MI is seen for a colectomy. What is the main goal of your cardiac assessment?
options: Baseline, active disease, risk, and monitoring plan
Diagnose all coronary disease before any surgery
Obtain cardiology clearance for any cardiac history at all
Avoid elective surgery in every patient with known CAD
questions.explanation: Cardiac assessment establishes baseline function, identifies active conditions, estimates risk, and guides monitoring and optimization.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which findings are red flags requiring evaluation before elective surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Red flags include active angina, recent MI, decompensated HF, symptomatic arrhythmia, severe symptomatic valvular disease, unexplained syncope, and new symptoms.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Four cases are booked for patients with similar CAD. Which procedure carries the HIGHEST cardiac risk?
options: Superficial skin excision under local anesthesia
questions.explanation: Major vascular and prolonged intrathoracic or intra-abdominal procedures are high cardiac risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with CAD and 3 METs is scheduled for one of four procedures. Which procedure carries the LOWEST cardiac risk?
questions.explanation: Cataract surgery is low cardiac risk; major vascular and prolonged intrathoracic or intra-abdominal cases are high risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient's last cardiology note is 2 years old, and he now reports increasing dyspnea on exertion. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Obtain updated cardiac evaluation before elective surgery
Proceed, since a cardiology note exists on file
Proceed with regional anesthesia to limit stress
Proceed after a normal resting ECG this morning in holding
questions.explanation: New or worsening symptoms are red flags; a recent cardiology note or evaluation is needed.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A 68-year-old on amiodarone with a prior MI has a preop ECG. What should you review on it?
options: Rhythm, conduction, infarct patterns, ischemia, and QT
Axis and voltage, since rhythm is on the monitor
Rate and rhythm, since ischemia needs echo
P waves and QRS width, since QT is not relevant
questions.explanation: ECG review covers rhythm, conduction, prior infarct, ischemic changes, QT (relevant with amiodarone), and pacing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient with a BMS placed 3 weeks ago is scheduled for elective cholecystectomy. What is the BEST decision?
options: Delay until more than 30 days after BMS
Proceed if DAPT is continued through surgery
Delay 6 months, the same as after CABG
questions.explanation: BMS requires >30 days before elective surgery.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient had a stent placed 4 months ago and takes aspirin and ticagrelor. What type of stent is MOST likely?
options: A drug-eluting stent requiring dual antiplatelet therapy
A bare metal stent requiring no antiplatelets
A stent whose DAPT stopped right after PCI
A CABG graft that is managed with dual antiplatelets
questions.explanation: Patients with drug-eluting stents are maintained on DAPT, which shapes surgical timing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which preop cardiac note BEST describes a patient who needs no further cardiac workup before an intermediate-risk case?
options: RRR, no JVD, >4 METs, BP controlled
Irregular rhythm, holosystolic murmur, and JVD
Tachycardia with an S3 and crackles
Bradycardia with a gallop and leg edema
questions.explanation: A normal exam, good capacity, controlled hypertension, and no active conditions support proceeding without more testing.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient has stable angina with exertion that has not changed for 3 years and ≥4 METs. Which is MOST appropriate?
options: Proceed with elective surgery with standard monitoring
Cancel for urgent catheterization before surgery
questions.explanation: Stable angina with good capacity and no change is not an active condition.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Which physical findings suggest heart failure per the cardiac history notes? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Heart failure signs include JVD, crackles, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, and fluid overload.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient has an MI treated with PCI 2 months ago. Which detail MOST changes your plan?
options: Whether a BMS or DES was placed
Whether the MI was inferior or anterior
questions.explanation: Timing rules differ for BMS (>30 days) and DES (3–6 months).
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Two patients have BP 168/98. One is asymptomatic; the other reports headaches, blurred vision, and new proteinuria. Why does this difference matter?
options: The asymptomatic patient is at higher risk
questions.explanation: Symptoms of end-organ dysfunction raise risk and may warrant delay, while asymptomatic BP under 180/110 does not independently predict risk.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A family member asks how serious "just high blood pressure" is. Which statement is accurate?
options: It contributes to ~0.5 million deaths yearly
It affects fewer than 1% of adults
It is uncommon in surgical patients under 65 years old
It causes fewer deaths each year than asthma does
questions.explanation: Hypertension is extremely common and contributes to about half a million deaths per year.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: A patient's preop BP is 134/86 on repeat. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 is 130–139/80–89. Elevated is 120–129 with diastolic under 80.
questions.topic: Ischemic heart disease, testing, and hypertension

questions.stem: Four patients with heart murmurs are scheduled for elective surgery. Which valve lesion carries the MOST perioperative concern?
questions.explanation: Severe AS (area under 1 cm²) carries the greatest concern because of perioperative sudden death risk.

questions.stem: An echo shows aortic valve area 0.8 cm², mean gradient 44 mmHg, and peak velocity 4.2 m/s. How is this graded, and what does it imply?
options: Moderate AS, with low perioperative risk
Mild AS, with no special precautions
questions.explanation: Valve area under 1.0 cm² defines severe AS, which carries high risk of hemodynamic collapse and sudden death.

questions.stem: A patient's echo shows AS with jet velocity 4.3 m/s and mean gradient 46 mmHg. How is this graded?
questions.explanation: Velocity ≥4 m/s and gradient ≥40 mmHg meet severe criteria.

questions.stem: An echo shows AS with velocity 3.4 m/s, gradient 28 mmHg, area 1.2 cm². Which grade is this?
questions.explanation: Moderate AS is velocity 3.0–3.9, gradient 20–39, and area 1.0–1.5 cm².

questions.stem: What does the note on the AS grading slide say about severe AS?
questions.explanation: The note says severe AS means high risk of an intraoperative event.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old has a known valve lesion and is scheduled for a hip replacement. What information is MOST important to review?
options: Echo and catheterization reports and current symptoms
The murmur description and the ECG findings alone
questions.explanation: Valvular disease assessment relies on echo, cath data, and symptoms.

questions.stem: A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border of a 78-year-old with exertional dyspnea. Which lesion pairing makes up the systolic group this murmur belongs to?
questions.explanation: MR and AS are systolic (MRASS); MS and AR are diastolic (MSARD). A RUSB crescendo-decrescendo murmur suggests AS.

questions.stem: Which murmur is holosystolic at the apex and radiates to the axilla?
questions.explanation: MR is holosystolic at the apex and radiates to the axilla.

questions.stem: Which murmur is midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, at the second parasternal interspace, radiating to the carotids?
questions.explanation: AS produces a crescendo-decrescendo midsystolic murmur at the second interspace radiating to the carotids.

questions.stem: Which murmur has an opening snap and a low-pitched middiastolic rumble at the apex?
questions.explanation: MS produces an opening snap and middiastolic rumble at the apex.

questions.stem: A murmur gets louder with Valsalva and standing and softer with squatting. Which lesion fits?
options: Aortic insufficiency with wide pulse pressure
questions.explanation: HCM and MVP increase with Valsalva/standing; AS decreases with Valsalva. The table lists HCM as midsystolic at the apex/LLSB.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with heart failure has an EF of 58% on echo. How is this classified?
options: HFpEF, carrying lower perioperative risk than HFrEF
Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction
Normal function with no heart failure
questions.explanation: HFpEF is EF above 50% and lower risk than HFrEF (EF under about 49%).

questions.stem: Two heart failure patients are scheduled for the same surgery: one with EF 58%, one with EF 32%. Which carries higher perioperative risk?
options: Neither, since EF does not affect risk
questions.explanation: HFrEF carries higher perioperative risk than HFpEF.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old with ischemic cardiomyopathy comes for preop evaluation. Which findings suggest decompensated LV dysfunction? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Signs of LV dysfunction include dyspnea, pulmonary edema, tachypnea, tachycardia, and JVD.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has insulin-treated diabetes, a creatinine of 2.4, prior MI, and is scheduled for an open colectomy. How many RCRI points does she have?
questions.explanation: Insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine above 2.0, ischemic heart disease, and intraperitoneal surgery each add 1 point, for 4.

questions.stem: Three patients have creatinines of 1.4, 1.9, and 2.3 mg/dL. Which one earns an RCRI point for renal function?
options: All three, since each is above normal
questions.explanation: The RCRI renal criterion is creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL.

questions.stem: Patient A controls diabetes with metformin and diet. Patient B uses glargine and lispro. Which patient earns an RCRI point for diabetes?
options: Patient A, since metformin implies severe disease
Both patients, since both have diabetes
Neither, since HbA1c determines the point
questions.explanation: Only diabetes requiring insulin earns an RCRI point.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on insulin with prior stroke and creatinine 2.4 is scheduled for open AAA repair. What is his RCRI score?
questions.explanation: Insulin DM (1), cerebrovascular disease (1), Cr >2.0 (1), suprainguinal vascular surgery (1) = 4.

questions.stem: What MACE risk corresponds to an RCRI score of 3 or more?
A 52-year-old with no RCRI risk factors is scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. What is her estimated risk of MACE?
questions.explanation: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is intraperitoneal, which is 1 RCRI point. With no other factors, her score is 1 and her MACE risk is about 1.0%.

questions.stem: Which surgeries count as high-risk in the RCRI? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: High-risk surgery includes intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular procedures.

questions.stem: A patient with stable CAD and CHF is having laparoscopic cholecystectomy. What is his RCRI score?
questions.explanation: IHD (1), CHF (1), and intraperitoneal surgery (1) = 3.

questions.stem: A patient has an RCRI of 0 but cannot climb stairs because of dyspnea and is ASA III. A colleague says, "RCRI is zero, so no further thought is needed." What is the flaw?
options: RCRI must be combined with METs and ASA
RCRI includes METs, so nothing else is needed
questions.explanation: RCRI is not a standalone tool; poor functional capacity and ASA status add important information.

questions.stem: A patient had an episode of pulmonary edema 2 years ago and now has an S3 and JVD. Which RCRI item does this satisfy?
questions.explanation: A history or signs of heart failure satisfy the RCRI congestive heart failure criterion.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with prior rheumatic fever has a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex. Which lesion pairing makes up the diastolic group?
questions.explanation: MS and AR are diastolic (MSARD). Rheumatic disease commonly causes mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: A blowing, holodiastolic murmur is heard at the third and fourth left parasternal spaces in a patient with a wide pulse pressure. Which lesion is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Aortic insufficiency produces a holodiastolic murmur at the left parasternal spaces with a wide pulse pressure.

questions.stem: A young woman has a midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur that moves earlier when she stands. Which lesion is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: A midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is characteristic of mitral valve prolapse.

questions.stem: In adult surgical patients with valvular heart disease, which lesions will you encounter MOST often?
questions.explanation: Aortic and mitral lesions are most common in adults.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with severe AS on an echo from 2 years ago is scheduled for elective hip replacement. What is the BEST next step?
options: Review current echo, cath, and symptoms
Proceed with spinal anesthesia without further review
Proceed if the murmur is soft today and BP is normal
questions.explanation: Severe AS is high risk. Current echo, cath data, and symptoms guide whether and how to proceed; spinal is often avoided.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with prior MI is scheduled for an open AAA repair (suprainguinal vascular). What is his RCRI score and MACE risk?
questions.explanation: Ischemic heart disease and high-risk surgery each add 1 point, for a score of 2 and about 2.4% MACE risk.

questions.stem: A patient had a TIA 6 months ago with full recovery. Which RCRI item does this satisfy?
questions.explanation: Prior stroke or TIA counts as cerebrovascular disease in the RCRI.

questions.stem: Four patients have arrhythmias on preop ECGs. Which one represents a generally benign finding for elective surgery?
options: SVT requiring antiarrhythmics with recent recurrence
New atrial fibrillation with RVR at 140
Nonsustained VT with a family history of sudden death
questions.explanation: Rate-controlled AF, PVCs, and PACs are generally benign.

questions.stem: Four patients report arrhythmia histories. Which one is potentially malignant and warrants further evaluation before elective surgery?
options: SVT on flecainide with sudden death history
Occasional PACs found on a routine ECG
Rate-controlled atrial fibrillation at 72 on metoprolol
questions.explanation: SVT requiring antiarrhythmics, or a family history of sudden death, labels a history potentially malignant. Rate-controlled AF, PACs, and isolated PVCs are generally benign.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old reports palpitations that started 2 days ago, and his ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 132. He is scheduled for an elective knee replacement. What is the BEST plan?
options: Postpone for a cardiac workup of the new arrhythmia
Proceed with rate control in the OR
Proceed, since AF is a benign rhythm
Proceed after one dose of metoprolol in preop
questions.explanation: New-onset AF needs a cardiac workup before elective surgery.

questions.stem: What must you know about a patient's CIED before surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The CIED slide lists device type, programming, indication, dependence, last interrogation, function, shocks, and magnet response.

questions.stem: During a case with monopolar cautery near a pacemaker, the device inhibits and the HR falls to 30. You need to place a magnet. What should you have known before the case?
questions.explanation: A magnet is usually in the OR; knowing its location and the device's magnet response lets you act quickly when EMI causes inhibition.

questions.stem: A patient with a pacemaker is having surgery near the generator with monopolar cautery. Why is this a concern?
options: EMI can inhibit or disrupt device function
Cautery turns off the device permanently
EMI affects ICDs but not pacemakers
questions.explanation: EMI from monopolar cautery near the generator can inhibit pacing or trigger inappropriate therapy.

questions.stem: Which pacemaker mode is the most common backup mode and often used perioperatively?
questions.explanation: VVI is ventricular paced, sensed, inhibited, and is the most common backup mode.

questions.stem: A patient with sick sinus syndrome and intact AV conduction has a pacemaker. Later he develops complete heart block. Which pacing mode would now FAIL to maintain ventricular rate?
questions.explanation: AAI paces only the atrium and relies on intact AV conduction; with complete heart block, atrial impulses no longer reach the ventricles.

questions.stem: A pacemaker-dependent patient is having a laparotomy with monopolar cautery near the abdomen. Which mode is used temporarily to prevent EMI from inhibiting pacing?
questions.explanation: Asynchronous modes such as VOO pace at a fixed rate regardless of sensed activity, so cautery cannot inhibit them.

questions.stem: You place a magnet over a dual-chamber pacemaker in a pacemaker-dependent patient. The rhythm changes to fixed-rate pacing of both chambers. Which mode is this?
questions.explanation: A magnet converts many dual-chamber pacemakers to DOO, asynchronous pacing of atrium and ventricle.

questions.stem: A patient with complete heart block has a dual-chamber pacemaker that senses the atrium and paces the ventricle after each P wave. Which mode preserves this AV synchrony?
questions.explanation: DDD paces and senses both chambers, maintaining AV synchrony; it is very common.

questions.stem: Which mode senses both atrium and ventricle but paces the ventricle only?
questions.explanation: VDD senses atrium and ventricle and paces the ventricle only, preserving AV synchrony.

questions.stem: A patient's pacemaker is set to DDDR. During exercise his paced rate rises from 70 to 110. What does the "R" add?
options: Rate response that increases HR with activity
Reverse pacing from ventricle to atrium
questions.explanation: Rate response increases the pacing rate with activity sensed by the device.

questions.stem: Which tachyarrhythmia therapies are provided by an ICD? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: ICD tachy therapies include ATP, cardioversion, and defibrillation.

questions.stem: Which facts about an ICD must the anesthesia provider know? (Select 2)
options: Whether tachy therapies are active or suspended
The name of the hospital where it was implanted
The date the leads were placed
questions.explanation: You need to know pacemaker dependence and whether tachy therapies are active or suspended. Recent shocks matter too, but implant details and warranty do not change management.

questions.stem: A patient with an ICD cannot say why it was placed or when the battery was changed. What do the notes suggest?
options: No concern if the device is working
Proceed with magnet placement without records
Assume the device is a pacemaker
questions.explanation: The notes say no answer may signal noncompliance, so get device records and interrogation data.

questions.stem: A patient has an ICD and you review the interrogation report. Which bradycardia pacing modes are typically programmed in ICDs?
questions.explanation: ICDs are often programmed for bradycardia pacing as VVI, DDD, or AAI. Asynchronous modes are used intraoperatively when needed.

questions.stem: A pacemaker's lower rate is 60 and an ICD's VT detection rate is 170. During surgery, the HR rises to 175 from sinus tachycardia. Why does knowing these settings matter?
options: Sinus tachycardia could trigger a shock
Knowing the rates determines the ETT size
questions.explanation: Low and high rates define pacing and therapy thresholds; sinus tachycardia above the detection rate could trigger an inappropriate shock.

questions.stem: A patient's ICD was last interrogated 3 years ago, and he reports two shocks last month. Why is the interrogation date important?
options: It confirms current function and settings
It matters for pacemakers, not ICDs
questions.explanation: A recent interrogation confirms function and settings; an old one plus recent shocks means the device needs evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient with an ICD is having surgery with monopolar cautery above the umbilicus. Which question is specific to ICDs?
options: Is the device programmed in a rate-responsive mode?
questions.explanation: ICDs require a plan to suspend tachyarrhythmia therapies, by magnet or reprogramming, to prevent inappropriate shocks from EMI.

questions.stem: A patient with a CIED is having a hand procedure without cautery. Which question is LEAST relevant?
options: Is the surgical site near the pulse generator?
Is the patient pacemaker dependent for every beat?
What is the indication for the device?
questions.explanation: Site proximity mainly matters with EMI sources like cautery; dependence, interrogation, and indication still matter.

questions.stem: Which question MOST helps plan for EMI during surgery?
options: Is the patient taking dual antiplatelet therapy?
questions.explanation: Monopolar cautery is a major EMI source that can affect CIEDs.

questions.stem: A preop clinic sees four patients with CIEDs this week. Which type of device is MOST likely to be the most common?
questions.explanation: The pacemaker is the most common CIED.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with COPD has spirometry showing an FEV1/FVC of 0.55. What does this indicate for anesthesia?
options: Obstruction with low reserve and bronchospasm risk
Normal flow with small lung volumes
Fully reversible obstruction with no added risk
questions.explanation: A low FEV1/FVC indicates obstruction, low reserve, and bronchospasm risk.

questions.stem: A COPD patient's room-air ABG is pH 7.37, PaCO2 52, PaO2 62, HCO3 30. He feels at his baseline. How should you interpret this?
options: Chronic compensated hypercarbia with baseline hypoxemia
A normal ABG for his age
questions.explanation: COPD patients may live with chronic hypercarbia and hypoxemia; the normal pH and high HCO3 show renal compensation.

questions.stem: A COPD patient's chest X-ray is reviewed before surgery. Which findings would be typical of his disease?
options: A deep sulcus sign of pneumothorax
questions.explanation: COPD films may show bullae, hyperlucency, or effusions. Bullae matter for nitrous oxide and positive pressure.

questions.stem: A COPD patient is wheezing in preop, and his last inhaler dose was 18 hours ago. What is the BEST step before induction?
options: Proceed and treat the wheeze after intubation
Deepen induction with volatile to bronchodilate
questions.explanation: A tune-up aerosol before induction reduces bronchospasm risk during airway instrumentation.

questions.stem: Which information about inhalers should you obtain? (Select 3)
options: When the last dose was taken
questions.explanation: The slide asks what inhalers, how frequent, and when last taken.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old's wheezing resolves completely after albuterol. Which condition does this BEST fit?
questions.explanation: Asthma is reversible airflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with asthma is scheduled for surgery. Which history items are known asthma triggers? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Asthma triggers include exercise, allergens, infections, and emotional stress.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with asthma uses fluticasone and albuterol. What should she do with these before surgery?
options: Continue them through the morning of surgery
Hold the inhaled steroid the morning of surgery
Start oral steroids the day of surgery
questions.explanation: The goal is to keep asthma patients on their medications up to surgery.

questions.stem: An asthmatic reports a prednisone taper last month. Which issue should you consider?
options: Possible HPA axis suppression and stress-dose steroids
Increased MAC from chronic steroid use
Lower glucose from steroid withdrawal during fasting
questions.explanation: Recent steroids raise concern for adrenal suppression; the asthma slide asks what to consider after recent steroid therapy.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has bronchospasm triggered by stress, and she is very anxious in preop. Why might an anxiolytic be part of her asthma plan?
questions.explanation: Emotional stress is an asthma trigger, so reducing anxiety can help prevent bronchospasm.

questions.stem: How long should elective adult surgery be delayed after a URI?
questions.explanation: Airway hyperreactivity can last up to 6 weeks, so best practice is to delay elective adult cases 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has clear rhinorrhea, no fever, and normal activity on the day of ear tube placement. What is the BEST plan?
options: Proceed, since he is afebrile and mildly symptomatic
Delay 6 weeks, as recommended for adults with URI
Proceed after a clear chest X-ray
questions.explanation: Children have frequent URIs, and proceeding is generally safe if they are afebrile and not significantly symptomatic.

questions.stem: Why is a 6-week delay after URI often not feasible in children?
options: Children do not have airway hyperreactivity
Children require GA for all procedures
questions.explanation: Frequent URIs in children make a 6-week delay impractical.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with a BMI of 41 snores loudly and is scheduled for a hernia repair. Which pulmonary screening steps apply? (Select 3)
options: Asking about diagnosed OSA and CPAP use
Peak flow testing in all patients
Arterial blood gas in every patient
questions.explanation: Pulmonary screening includes STOP-BANG, OSA and CPAP history, and at least listening to the heart and lungs.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man snores loudly, is tired during the day, has hypertension, a BMI of 33, and a neck circumference of 42 cm. No one has observed apneas. What is his STOP-BANG score?
questions.explanation: Snoring, tiredness, pressure, age over 50, neck over 40 cm, and male sex score 6. BMI 33 is below 35 and no apneas were observed.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a BMI of 37, a neck circumference of 38 cm, and treated hypertension. Which STOP-BANG thresholds does she meet?
questions.explanation: She meets BMI over 35 and pressure. Age 48 is not over 50, and 38 cm is not over 40 cm.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with snoring, treated HTN, and BMI 32 is screened. What is his STOP-BANG score?
questions.explanation: Snoring (1), pressure (1), age >50 (1), male (1) = 4. BMI 32 does not meet >35.

questions.stem: A patient scores 4 on STOP-BANG. How should this shape your plan?
options: Intermediate risk; plan for possible OSA with caution
No interpretation possible without a sleep study
questions.explanation: A STOP-BANG of 3–4 is intermediate risk, which should prompt caution with sedatives and opioids.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman who snores, is tired, has observed apnea, HTN, and BMI 37. What is her STOP-BANG risk?
questions.explanation: S, T, O, P, B, A = 6 points. Female sex does not score. 6 is high risk.

questions.stem: A thin 35-year-old woman who does not snore has a STOP-BANG of 1 (tiredness). How should you classify her?
options: Low risk, since 0–2 is low risk
Unable to classify without a sleep study
questions.explanation: A STOP-BANG score of 0–2 is low risk for OSA.

questions.stem: Which STOP-BANG items relate to physical measurement? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: BMI, age, and neck circumference are measured or demographic; snoring, tiredness, and apnea are symptoms.

questions.stem: A COPD patient with FEV1/FVC 55% is scheduled for an open colectomy. Which intraoperative risk is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Low FEV1/FVC signals obstruction, low reserve, and bronchospasm risk.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old says he quit cigarettes but now vapes daily. Which statement about his pulmonary assessment is accurate?
options: Vaping is declining as smoking increases
